summary: A multiplayer game is a game that begins with more than two players.
These rules consist of a series of options that can be added to a multiplayer game and a number of variant styles of multiplayer play.
Many multiplayer Magic tournaments have additional rules not included here, including rules for deck construction.
Unlike two-player games, multiplayer games can continue after one or more players have left the game.
When a player leaves the game, all objects (see rule 109) owned by that player leave the game and any effects which give that player control of any objects or players end.
If an object would change to the control of a player who has left the game, it doesn’t.

If an effect that gives a player still in the game control of an object ends, there is no other effect giving control of that object to another player in the game, and the player who controlled that object by default has left the game, the object is exiled.
If an object that would be owned by a player who has left the game would be created in any zone, it isn’t created.
If combat damage would be assigned to a player who has left the game, that damage isn’t assigned.
If an object requires a player who has left the game to pay a cost or choose whether to pay a cost, that cost is not paid.
If an object requires a player who has left the game to make a choice other than whether to pay a cost, the controller of the object chooses another player to make that choice.
If a rule requires a player who has left the game to make a choice, the next player in turn order makes that choice.

If an effect requires information about a specific player, the effect uses the current information about that player if they are still in the game; otherwise, the effect uses the last known information about that player before they left the game.
If a player leaves the game during their turn, that turn continues to its completion without an active player.
If a player who has left the game would begin a turn, that turn doesn’t begin.
When a player leaves the game, any continuous effects with durations that last until that player’s next turn or until a specific point in that turn will last until that turn would have begun.
When a player leaves the game, objects that player owns in the ante zone do not leave the game.

In a Planechase game, if the player designated as the planar controller would leave the game, instead the next player in turn order that wouldn’t leave the game becomes the planar controller, then the old planar controller leaves the game.
Unless a chosen variant or option prescribes otherwise, seating order is determined by any mutually agreeable method.
In a multiplayer game, the first mulligan a player takes doesn’t count toward the number of cards that player will put on the bottom of their library or the number of mulligans that player may take.
In a multiplayer game other than a Two-Headed Giant game, the starting player doesn’t skip the draw step of their first turn.
Limited range of influence is an option that can be applied to most multiplayer games.
A player’s range of influence is the maximum distance from that player, measured in player seats, that the player can affect.
The most commonly chosen limited ranges of influence are 1 seat and 2 seats.
A player is always within their own range of influence.
The particular players within each player’s range of influence are determined as each turn begins.
An object is within a player’s range of influence if it’s controlled by that player or by another player within that many seats of that player.
Creatures can attack only opponents within their controller’s range of influence, planeswalkers controlled by those opponents, and battles protected by those opponents.
Objects and players outside a player’s range of influence can’t be the targets of spells or abilities that player controls.
Some cards require players to make choices.
If a player is asked to choose an object or player, they must choose one within their range of influence.

If a player is asked to choose between one or more options (and not between one or more objects or players), they can choose between those options even if those options refer to objects or players outside the player’s range of influence.
If an effect requires a choice and there’s no player who can make that choice within its controller’s range of influence, the closest appropriate player to its controller’s left makes that choice.
A player can’t activate the activated abilities of an object outside of their range of influence.
A triggered ability doesn’t trigger unless its trigger event happens entirely within the range of influence of its source’s controller.

If a trigger event includes an object moving out of or into a player’s range of influence, use the game state before or after the event as appropriate to determine whether the triggered ability will trigger.
An Aura can’t enchant an object or player outside its controller’s range of influence.
An Equipment can’t equip an object outside its controller’s range of influence, and a Fortification can’t fortify an object outside its controller’s range of influence.
Spells and abilities can’t affect objects or players outside their controller’s range of influence.
If a spell or ability requires information from the game, it gets only information from within its controller’s range of influence.
The “world rule” (see rule 704.5k) applies to a permanent only if other world permanents are within its controller’s range of influence.
Replacement and prevention effects watch for a particular event to happen and then completely or partially replace that event.
If a replacement effect tries to cause a spell or ability to affect an object or player outside its controller’s range of influence, that portion of the event does nothing.
If a spell or ability creates an effect that prevents damage that would be dealt by a source, it can affect only sources within the spell or ability’s controller’s range of influence.
If an effect states that a player wins the game, all of that player’s opponents within that player’s range of influence lose the game instead.
If the effect of a spell or ability states that the game is a draw, the game is a draw for that spell or ability’s controller and all players within that player’s range of influence.

If the game somehow enters a “loop” of mandatory actions, repeating a sequence of events with no way to stop, the game is a draw for each player who controls an object that’s involved in that loop, as well as for each player within the range of influence of any of those players.
Effects that restart the game (see rule 727) are exempt from the limited range of influence option.
In multiplayer Planechase games other than Grand Melee games, plane cards and phenomenon cards are exempt from the limited range of influence option.
Some multiplayer games allow the active player to attack multiple other players.
As the combat phase starts, the attacking player doesn’t choose an opponent to become the defending player.
Any rule, object, or effect that refers to a “defending player” refers to one specific defending player, not to all of the defending players.

As the attacking player declares each attacking creature, they choose a defending player, a planeswalker controlled by a defending player, or a battle protected by a defending player for it to attack.
Restrictions and requirements that don’t apply to attacking a specific player are evaluated based on the entire group of attacking creatures.
Creatures in a band can’t attack different players.

If more than one player is being attacked, controls a planeswalker that’s being attacked, or protects a battle that’s being attacked, each defending player in APNAP order declares blockers as the declare blockers step begins.
A defending player can block only with creatures they control.
When determining whether a defending player’s blocks are legal, ignore any creatures attacking other players and any blocking creatures controlled by other players.
Combat damage is assigned in APNAP order.

rule_group_title: Attack Left and Attack Right Options
summary: Some multiplayer games use the optional attack left or attack right rules.

rule_group_title: Attack Left and Attack Right Options
summary: If the attack left option is used, a player can attack only an opponent seated immediately to their left, a planeswalker that player controls, or a battle that player protects.

rule_group_title: Attack Left and Attack Right Options
summary: If the attack right option is used, a player can attack only an opponent seated immediately to their right, a planeswalker that player controls, or a battle that player protects.
The Emperor variant always uses the deploy creatures option, and it can be used in other variants that allow players to compete in teams.
Each creature has the ability “{T}: Target teammate gains control of this creature.
Some multiplayer games between teams use the shared team turns option.
Within each team, the player seated in the rightmost seat from that team’s perspective is the primary player.
The methods described in rule 103.1 are used to determine which team will take the first turn.
The process for handling mulligans is altered accordingly.
The process for handling cards that allow a player to begin the game with them on the battlefield is altered accordingly.
Each team takes turns rather than each player.
The team whose turn it is is the active team.
Each player on a team draws a card during that team’s draw step.
Each player on a team may play a land during each of that team’s turns.
An ability that triggers at the beginning of a step or phase may trigger multiple times if it triggers at the beginning of “each player’s” or “each opponent’s” step or phase.
Teams have priority, not individual players.
A player may cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action when their team has priority.
If a team has priority and no player on that team wishes to do anything, that team passes.
The Active Player, Nonactive Player order rule (see rule 101.4) is modified if the shared team turns option is used.

If more than one player is instructed to draw cards in a game that’s using the shared team turns option, first each player on the active team, in whatever order that team likes, performs that player’s draws, then each player on each nonactive team in turn order does the same.

If multiple triggered abilities have triggered since the last time a team received priority, the members of the active team put all triggered abilities any of them controls on the stack in any order they choose, then the members of each nonactive team in turn order do the same.
If an effect gives a player an extra turn or adds a phase or step to that player’s turn, that player’s team takes the extra turn, phase, or step.
Any ability that refers to the “active player” refers to one specific active player, not to all of the active players.
The shared team turns option uses different combat rules than other multiplayer options.
Each team’s creatures attack the other team as a group.
As the declare attackers step begins, the active team declares attackers.
Any rule, object, or effect that refers to an “attacking player” refers to one specific attacking player, not to all attacking players.
As the declare blockers step begins, the defending team declares blockers.
Any rule, object, or effect that refers to a “defending player” refers to one specific defending player, not to all of the defending players.
As the combat damage step begins, the active team announces how each attacking creature will assign its combat damage.
In Free-for-All multiplayer games, a group of players compete as individuals against each other.
Any multiplayer options used are determined before play begins.
The limited range of influence option usually isn’t used in Free-for-All games.
Exactly one of the attack left, attack right, and attack multiple players options must be used.
The deploy creatures option isn’t used in the Free-for-All variant.
The players are randomly seated around the table.
The Grand Melee variant is a modification of the Free-for-All variant, in which a group of players compete against each other as individuals.
Any multiplayer options used are decided before play begins.
Each player has a range of influence of 1 (see rule 801).
The attack left option is used (see rule 803).
The attack multiple players and deploy creatures options aren’t used in the Grand Melee variant.
The players are seated at random.
The Grand Melee variant allows multiple players to take turns at the same time.
There is one turn marker for each full four players in the game.
The starting player in the game gets the first turn marker.
After a player ends their turn, that player passes the turn marker to the player on their left.
A player who receives a turn marker can’t begin their turn if any player in the three seats to their left has a turn marker.
If a player leaves the game and that player leaving the game would reduce the number of turn markers in the game, the turn marker immediately to the departed player’s right is designated for removal.
For the purposes of determining if one or more players leaving the game would reduce the number of turn markers in the game (see rule 807.4e), disregard turn markers already designated for removal.
If a player who’s taking a turn has a turn marker that’s been designated for removal, that turn marker is removed rather than being passed after that turn ends.
If one or more consecutively seated players leave the game, the players that were on either side of those seats don’t enter one another’s range of influence until the next turn begins.

If an effect causes a player with a turn marker to take an extra turn after the current one, that player keeps the turn marker and starts their next turn after the current turn ends, unless another turn marker is too close on either side at that time.

If an effect would cause a player to take an extra turn after the current turn, but that player wouldn’t have a turn marker at the start of that turn, that player will take the extra turn immediately before their next turn instead.
Rather than having a single stack, Grand Melee games contain multiple stacks.

A player gets priority for a particular turn marker’s stack only if the turn marker is within their range of influence or an object on that stack is controlled by a player within their range of influence.

If a player has priority for multiple stacks and casts a spell, activates an ability, or a triggered ability they control triggers, the player must specify which one of those stacks the spell or ability is put on.

Any multiplayer options used are determined before play begins.
The attack multiple players option is used (see rule 802).
The deploy creatures options and limited range of influence options usually aren’t used in the Team vs.

The Emperor variant involves two or more teams of three players each.
Each team sits together on one side of the table.
The Emperor variant uses the following default options.
The range of influence is limited to 2 for emperors and 1 for generals.
Emperor games use the deploy creatures option (see rule 804).

A player can attack only an opponent seated immediately next to them, a planeswalker controlled by a player seated immediately next to them, or a battle protected by a player seated immediately next to them.
Randomly determine which emperor goes first.
The Emperor variant includes the following specifications for winning and losing the game.
A team wins the game if its emperor wins.
A team loses the game if its emperor loses.
The game is a draw for a team if the game is a draw for its emperor.
The Emperor variant can also be played with any number of equally sized teams.
Each general’s range of influence should be the minimum number that allows one general from an opposing team to begin the game within their range of influence.
In the Emperor variant, a team’s resources (cards in hand, mana, and so on) are not shared.
Two-Headed Giant games are played with two teams of two players each.
The Two-Headed Giant variant uses the shared team turns option.
Each team sits together on one side of the table.
Each team has a shared life total, which starts at 30 life.
With the exception of life total and poison counters, a team’s resources (cards in hand, mana, and so on) are not shared in the Two-Headed Giant variant.
The team who plays first skips the draw step of its first turn.
The Two-Headed Giant variant uses the combat rules for the shared team turns option (see rule 805.10).
The Two-Headed Giant variant uses the normal rules for winning or losing the game (see rule 104), with the following additions and specifications.
Players win and lose the game only as a team, not as individuals.
If a player concedes, their team leaves the game immediately.
If a team’s life total is 0 or less, the team loses the game.
If a team has fifteen or more poison counters, that team loses the game.
Damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually.
If a cost or effect needs to know the value of an individual player’s life total, that cost or effect uses the team’s life total instead.
If a cost or effect allows both members of a team to pay life simultaneously, the total amount of life they pay may not exceed their team’s life total.
If an effect sets a single player’s life total to a specific number, the player gains or loses the necessary amount of life to end up with the new total.
If an effect would set the life total of each player on a team to a number, that team chooses one of its members.
A player can’t exchange life totals with their teammate.
If an effect instructs a player to redistribute any number of players’ life totals, that player may not affect more than one member of each team this way.
If an effect says that a player can’t gain life, no player on that player’s team can gain life.
If an effect says that a player can’t lose life, no player on that player’s team can lose life or pay any amount of life other than 0.
Effects that cause players to get poison counters happen to each player individually.
If an effect needs to know how many poison counters an individual player has, that effect uses the number of poison counters that player’s team has.
If an effect says that a player loses poison counters, that player’s team loses that many poison counters.
If an effect says that a player can’t get poison counters, no player on that player’s team can get poison counters.
If a rule or effect needs to know what kinds of counters an individual player has, that effect uses the kinds of counters that player has and the kinds of counters that player’s team has.
The Two-Headed Giant variant can also be played with equally sized teams of more than two players.
Alternating Teams games are played with two or more teams of equal size.
Any multiplayer options used are determined before play begins.
The recommended range of influence is 2.
Exactly one of the attack left, attack right, and attack multiple players options must be used.
The deploy creatures option isn’t normally used in the Alternating Teams variant.
At the start of the game, players are seated so that no one is next to a teammate and each team is equally spaced out.

A player can’t attack opponents who aren’t seated next to them, planeswalkers that aren’t controlled by opponents seated next to them, or battles that aren’t protected by opponents seated next to them.
In the Alternating Teams variant, a team’s resources (cards in hand, mana, and so on) are not shared.
